name: Unit 10 - Galen System Focused Review - Neurological Student

slides.title: Anatomy of the Brain
text: Recognize size, shape and texture of objects

slides.title: Occipital lobe
text: Responsible for coordination of movement, balance, proprioception & integration of sensory input

slides.title: Brain stem
text: Midbrain: connects pons & cerebellum w/ hemispheres sensory & motor pathways, center for auditory & visual reflexes, CN III & IV
Pons: bridge b/t various structures, CN V – VIII, motor & sensory pathways, control of HR,R, BP
Medulla oblongata: motor fibers from brain to spinal cord & sensory fibers from spinal cord to brain, CN IX - XII

slides.title: Cerebral Circulation
text: Brain receives 750-800 mL blood/minute or 15-20% of total resting cardiac output
High metabolic demand; no nutrient storage
Arteries fill from below; veins (no valves) drain from above, do not follow arterial circulation; poor collateral flow
2 pairs of major neck arteries/veins : 2 internal carotids, 2 vertebral
Circle of Willis: base of brain, ring of arteries; can provide some collateral flow if blockage; site for aneurysm

slides.title: Cranial Nerves
text: Sensory to head & face, motor for chewing, tongue
VI Abducens (work with nerves III & IV)
Motor to most facial muscles, facial expression

slides.title: VIII Vestibulocochlear
text: Taste, motor swallowing , sensory to tongue and throat
Most of abdominal & thoracic organs, gag reflex

slides.title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
text: Temporary neurologic deficit resulting from a temporary impairment of blood flow
Lasts < 24 hours, most resolve in < 1 hour
Sudden loss motor, sensory, visual function

slides.title: Stroke
text: Stroke is the primary cerebrovascular disorder and the third leading cause of death in the U.S.
Sudden loss of function resulting from a disruption of the blood supply to a part of the brain

slides.title: Prevention
text: Smoking and drug and alcohol abuse

slides.title: Tests to Diagnose CVA
text: Single most important diagnostic test for possible CVA
CT within 25 minutes of arrival to ED, read in another 20 minutes, treat in 1 hour
May appear normal for few hours initially
Ischemic brain is damaged and usually begins to swell after 6-12 hours.

slides.title: 15-item neurologic examination stroke scale used to evaluate the effect of acute cerebral infarction
text: 15-item neurologic examination stroke scale used to evaluate the effect of acute cerebral infarction
Ratings for each item are scored with 3 to 5 grades with 0 as normal, and there is an allowance for untestable items.
The single client assessment requires less than 10 minutes to complete
National Institute of Health Stroke Scale

slides.title: Stroke Interventions
text: Most important is to find out when was the onset of symptoms
Rapid transport to certified stroke center
No dextrose fluids or hypertonic fluids

slides.title: Cerebrovascular Terms
text: Hemiplegia (paralysis of one side of the body)
Hemiparesis  (weakness of one side of the body)
Dysarthria (disturbance in the muscular control of speech)
Apraxia (loss of the ability to execute skilled movements and gestures)
Expressive aphasia (loss of ability to produce language)

slides.title: Cerebrovascular Terms
text: A loss of vision in half of the visual field of one eye or both eyes

slides.title: Ischemic Stroke
text: Disruption of the blood supply due to an obstruction that causes infarction of brain tissue
Symptoms depend upon location & size of affected area
Recovery – depends on location and size of infarction after edema has disappeared

slides.title: Manifestations of Ischemic Stroke
text: Numbness or weakness of face, arm, or leg, especially on one side
Confusion or change in mental status
Difficulty in walking, dizziness, or loss of balance or coordination

slides.title: Treatment
text: Health maintenance measures including a healthy diet, exercise, and the prevention and treatment of periodontal disease
Antiplatelet therapy: aspirin, dipyridamole (Persantine), clopidogrel (Plavix), and ticlopidine (Ticlid)

slides.title: Hypertension Management
text: Treat Systolic BP >220 and Diastolic BP>120
NOTE:  BP usually decreases when ICP is controlled
Labetalol (Normodyne, Trandate) is antihypertensive of choice
Limited effect on cerebral vessels & no reflex tachycardia

slides.title: Thrombolytic Therapy
text: 3 – 4.5-hour window from s/s onset: ineligible if UNK
Once determined as candidate no other anticoagulants given for 24 hours
Bleeding common SE: assess all sites, avoid invasive procedures for 24 hours (insertion of catheter, NG, arterial lines, etc.)

slides.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke
text: Aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation (AVM-younger persons), certain meds
Risk factors: HTN, > 55, ETOH, male, phenylpropanolamine (PPA)
Increased mortality, greater deficits, increased recovery time vs. ischemic
Sudden severe HA, loss of consciousness, nuchal rigidity, visual disturbances
CT scan, lumbar puncture if no IICP

slides.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke Management
text: Vasospasm – complication; increased mortality post initial bleed (4-14 days)
Aneurysm clips, calcium channel blockers, “triple-H therapy”
Recombinant activated factor VII; reduce bleeding; med mgmt. primarily supportive
Bed rest, sedation, manage vasospasm, prevent re-bleed, codeine & acetaminophen
Complications: vasospasm, seizures, hydrocephalus, re-bleeding, hyponatremia

slides.title: Seizures
text: Generalized Seizures (20% of seizures) – begins in a widespread fashion in cerebral cortex, LOC affected
Entire cerebral cortex affected, aura may be present, Sudden LOC, unconscious
Tonic phase – generalized muscle stiffening usually < 1 min
Clonic phase – rapid jerking, do not remember anything after seizure

slides.title: Seizures
text: Partial Seizures (80% of seizures) Seizures in a localized part of the brain
Always start in one part of the cerebral cortex, but can spread and secondarily become generalized
Simple Partial – hand or mouth twitching, Lasts <1 minute, no LOC, may be dizzy or report unusual feeling, smell, sound or sight
Complex Partial – focal disturbance, may stare straight ahead, look around, lip smack, fidget with clothes or wander aimlessly; impaired LOC, little memory after seizure

slides.title: Seizures
text: Disorder characterized by chronic spontaneous seizure activity
Rapid seizures in which the client does not wake up

slides.title: Seizures Precautions
text: Rescue equipment: oxygen, oral airway, suction equipment, padding for side rails, saline lock
Assist with ambulating/transferring if at risk (reduce falls)
Not to place item in client’s mouth if seizure occurs

Teaching: not to restrain client during a seizure, lower to floor or bed, protect head, remove items near by (injury protection), provide privacy, side-lying position with head flexed slightly forward, loosen clothing

slides.title: Anticonvulsants
text: Run in large peripheral vein or via CVC
Can discolor and cause purple glove syndrome
Do not mix with D5W – precipitates
Never hold this drug if NPO
Give IV or IM per physician order
IV – give slowly – rate not > 2 mg/min
Dilute with equal volume of sterile H2O, NSS or D5W
Monitor respirations q 5-15 min and before each repeated IV dose.

slides.title: Anticonvulsants
text: If impossible, give slowly thru infusion tubing as near to vein as possible
Do not inject into small veins
Monitor respirations every 5-15 minutes and before each repeated IV dose

slides.title: Multiple Sclerosis
text: A chronic,  immune-mediated progressive demyelinating disease of the CNS
Small patches of demyelination in brain and spinal cord
Demyelination leads to disorder in transmission of nerve impulses
At first lesions are temporary, later permanent
What is the action of the myelin sheath?

slides.title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
text: Symptom management of muscle spasms, fatigue, ataxia, bowel & bladder control

slides.title: Multiple Sclerosis
text: MRI –  primary diagnostic tool for MS
Visualizes multiple plaques in brain and spinal cord
CT Scan – may reveal cerebral atrophic changes

slides.title: Multiple Sclerosis
text: Stable disease with intermittent treatment to steady progression

slides.title: Multiple Sclerosis
text: IV methylprednisolone followed by oral taper dose
Immune suppression to treat acute relapse & shorten its duration
Reduce relapse frequency, duration, plaque # & size
Interferon beta – 1a (Rebif) Avonex) give IM weekly
(Capoxone) glatiramer acetate give SQ every other day
Increases antigen specific suppressor T cells
Decreases plaque #, increases time b/t relapse
May take several months for immune response

slides.title: Multiple Sclerosis
text: Often see incoordination, clumsiness and ataxia
Teach to walk with feet wide apart
Extreme fatigue contributes to exacerbation of symptoms

slides.title: Myasthenia Gravis
text: Autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction
Antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors so a decrease results
Fluctuating weakness of the skeletal muscles
Initially, symptoms involve the eyes, eyelids, chewing, and swallowing
Increased weakness has the day progresses

slides.title: Myasthenia Gravis
text: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor stops breakdown of ACH
Given IV, 30 sec. after see muscle weakness & ptosis resolve
Atropine is antidote for Tensilon (bradycardia, diaphoresis, cramping)
CT scan to identify thymus enlargement

slides.title: Myasthenia Gravis
text: Inhibits breakdown of ACH & increases concentration of available ACH  at neuromuscular junction
May take up to 3 years for benefit
What is the most important thing to remember when administering Mestinon?
notes: Azathioprine works to suppress the immune system to dampen down symptoms of myasthenia.

slides.title: Myasthenia Gravis
text: Mestinon – gradual dose increase to reach therapeutic effect
Fewer side effects than other anticholinesterases
Many meds contraindicated because they will exacerbate symptoms
Anticholinesterase meds MUST BE GIVEN ON TIME
What will occur if Mestinon is NOT given on time?

slides.title: Myasthenia vs. Cholinergic Crisis
text: Client will go into respiratory failure
Client will be placed on Vent and IV Tensilon administered

slides.title: Myasthenia Gravis
text: Meds given on time, coincide mealtimes w/ peak effects of meds
Rest before meals to decrease fatigue
Sit up w/ meals, neck slightly flexed, soft foods
Energy conservation strategies; rest periods t/o day
Coincide activity w/ peak energy & strength
Tape eyelids if ptosis for short periods, use artificial tears; patches
Factors that exacerbate s/s & may cause crisis:
Emotional stress, infections (esp. resp.), some meds, high environmental temp

slides.title: Autoimmune disorder
text: Acute attack of peripheral nerve myelin
Doesn't affect cognitive function or LOC
Rapid demyelination may produce respiratory failure
Paresthesia, pain r/t sensory nerve demyelination
Diminished or absent reflexes progressing up from lower extremities

slides.title: Guillain-Barre Syndrome
text: Possible elective ET intubation before resp. failure
Plasmapheresis and IVIG to reduce circulating antibodies
Recovery rates vary but most clients recover completely

slides.title: Parkinson's Disease
text: Associated w/ decreased levels of dopamine
Leads to imbalance that affects voluntary movement

slides.title: Parkinson's Disease
text: Convert to dopamine in basal ganglia
Benefits most pronounced in first few years of use
More levodopa made available to the brain
May take weeks to months to see results
Delay in prescribing due to  SE and  decreased efficacy
Benefits wane; then SE become pronounced

slides.title: Parkinson's Disease
text: Walking techniques for safety and balance

slides.title: Amyotrophic Lateral  Sclerosis (ALS)- Lou Gehrig's Disease
text: Amyotrophic Lateral  Sclerosis (ALS)- Lou Gehrig's Disease
Leads to death 2-6 years after diagnosis
Motor neurons in the brain  and spinal cord gradually degenerate
Fatigue, limb muscle weakness, drooling, muscle wasting
Riluzole (Rilutek) may help slow the progression

slides.title: Intracranial Pressure
text: The rigid cranial vault contains brain tissue + blood volume + CSF
These contents remain in a state of pressure and volume equilibrium.
There is limited space for expansion
An increase in any one of the above results in reciprocal change in the other

slides.title: Causes of IICP
text: IICP results in progressive neurological deficiencies
Compression of brain tissue and structures interferes with blood supply to the involved area
Results in ischemia and anoxia of brain cells

slides.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure
text: LOC = assess wakefulness, orientation, ability to follow simple commands
With IICP = restless, drowsy, disoriented, unable to follow commands
Extremities =assess hand grasps, leg movement and strength.
Pupils = assess PERLA; normal findings  - PEARL at 4-5 mm.
With IICP = sluggish, nonreactive and dilated
Vital signs = assess BP, P, R.
With IICP = Cushing's Triad(increased systolic BP, wide pulse pressure, slow bounding pulse)

slides.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure
text: Early indication of IICP – change in LOC (lethargy)
Late signs of IICP – initially Cushing's Triad–decerebrate posturing and fixed pupils

slides.title: ICP Monitoring
text: Normal ICP reading – 0-15 mmHg with head elevated 30 degrees
Normal CPP is = 85 mmHg with a normal range of 60-90 mmHg.
Keep CPP above 50 mmHg for adequate oxygenation and neuro checks

slides.title: Medical Management of IICP
text: Priority for nurses is ongoing neuro assessment
CSF Drainage – even removal of 1-2 ml may dramatically decrease ICP.
Hyperventilate to constrict vessels – decreased ICP (#1 method used)
Prevent hypoxia and hypercapnia – decreased pO2 and increased pCO2 causes vasodilation

slides.title: Management of IICP
text: Pulls water from cerebral extracellular space into blood
Dehydrates brain and decreases cerebral edema
Watch for pulmonary edema and H2O intoxication
Only corticosteroid that crosses blood brain barrier
Monitor for Na+ and H2O retention
Slowly discontinue drug, makes client prone to infection, give PO with food, monitor blood sugar, watch for rebound effect

slides.title: Nursing Interventions for IICP
text: Positioning and turning – raise HOB 30-45 degrees
Logroll or use alternating pressure mattress to turn
Suctioning and repositioning consistently raise ICP significantly
Calm atmosphere and rest – all research emphasizes importance of rest between procedures to prevent cumulative IICP.  15-60-minute rest periods between activities
Restrict conversations,  use soothing voice, limit painful procedures, limit nontherapeutic touch

slides.title: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)trauma or damage to the spinal cord
text: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)trauma or damage to the spinal cord
Four times more often in males
Upper cervical spine injury common in child abuse

slides.title: Classification of SCI
text: American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale
Classifies according to the degree of sensory and motor function present after injury
Tetraplegia: loss of movement and sensation in all four extremities and the trunk, associated with injury to the cervical spinal cord.
Paraplegia: loss of motion and sensation in the lower extremities and all or part of the trunk as a result of damage to the thoracic or lumbar spinal cord or to the sacral root.

slides.title: Emergency Treatment
text: Treat as SCI victim until it is ruled out

slides.title: Spinal Shock
text: Sudden depression of reflex activity in spinal cord below level of injury.
Muscles below lesions are without sensation, paralyzed, and flaccid, and reflexes absent
Hypotension, bradycardia,  bowel distention & paralytic ileus, and no perspirations
Can occur within 1 hour of injury and usually lasts 3-6 weeks

Nursing interventions – hydration (start IV),  avoid vagal stimulation (suction), decrease cardiac workload (Valsalva, anxiety, breathing), Intermittent catheterization every 4 hours, glycerin suppository every morning after breakfast

slides.title: Autonomic DysreflexiaMedical Emergency
text: Severe pounding headache, increased BP, profuse diaphoresis, nausea, nasal congestion, and bradycardia
Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in clients with cord lesions above T6 after spinal shock subsides
Causes: distended bladder, bowel distention or impaction, stimulation of skin (pain, thermal stimuli, pressure ulcer)
What are the nursing interventions for this client?

slides.title: Visual Assessment
text: 20/20 means the client can read at 20 feet

slides.title: Conjunctivitis
text: May be viral or bacterial( pink eye)

slides.title: Highly contagious – stay at home
text: Eyes watery, swollen, red, photophobia, sandy sensation in eye,
Avoid sharing towels, linens, makeup, toys
Use new tissue to wipe eye each time
Discard all makeup used prior to onset of symptoms

slides.title: Glaucoma
text: Characterized by progressive nerve atrophy and loss of vision along with changes in IOP (intra ocular pressure)
Can clients with glaucoma receive beta blockers?
notes: Open can but closed can not

slides.title: Open Angle Glaucoma
text: Peripheral vision lost before central vision

slides.title: Closed Angle Glaucoma
text: Permanent blindness results if IOP untreated > 24-48 hours

slides.title: Treatment
text: Pilocarpine to reduce resistance  of aqueous humor flow
Education- chronic condition, no cure, maintain vision that is left

slides.title: Cataracts
text: Clouding or opacity within the lens which leads to gradual painless blurring and loss of vision
Secondary-UV light, long term corticosteroid use

slides.title: Cataracts
text: Unable to discriminate among color hues

slides.title: Post ECCE (extracapsular cataract extraction)
text: Wear eye shield/glasses post surgery till cleared by MD
Wipe eye from inner to outer canthus
Do not lift, push, pull anything > 5 lbs.
Light activities only – walking, reading, TV

slides.title: Retinal Detachment
text: 2 layers of the retina separate due to fluid or retraction
If untreated in 48 hours will result in blindness
Causes: degeneration, trauma, severe physical exertion
S/S: *curtain being pulled over eye*, floating spots, flashes of light, no complaints of pain
Tx: Cover both eyes w/patch; Surgery
Pt. Teach: Sedentary activities post op, no bending, no lifting, report signs of re-detachment immediately

slides.title: Trauma
text: Protect using metal shield or paper cup
Do not put pressure on the eye
Do not let client blow their nose

slides.title: Hearing Loss
text: Hearing conducted over 2 pathways: air & bone
Conductive loss – problem with conduction of sound impulses through external ear canal, eardrum, middle ear
Sensorineural – damage to cochlea or 8th cranial nerve secondary to loud noises
Presbycusis – hearing loss due to aging, develops gradually – hearing aids amplify sound but do not improve hearing.

slides.title: Prevention
text: Use of PPE - Monitor noise pollution
Monitor ototoxic drugs – may cause decreased hearing, deafness, tinnitus. Examples: diuretics, aminoglycosides, salicylates

slides.title: Otitis Media
text: May lead to necrosis of tympanic membrane if untreated
Instill ear drops – turn affected ear up, pull pinna up and back in adults (>age 3)
Kids pull down & forward and Adults pull up and back
Have client remain in position several minutes to allow medicine to go via gravity into proper place

slides.title: NGN NCLEX-RN Practice Question
text: The nurse in the community clinic is caring for a 70-year-old client who has been wearing new bilateral hearing aids for 2 weeks. Which of the following should the nurse include in the client’s care plan?
Check the client’s dexterity with hearing aid use.
Communicate with the client above the client’s eye level.
Speak with the client using loud, high-pitched tones.
Remind the client to take off the glasses while wearing hearing aids.
